rows.title: Managerial Accounting
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Perform cost-volume-profit analysis and prepare various budgets to provide management with relevant information in planning activities.
Use variance analysis and performance measurement methods to provide feedback about product, segment, management, and company performance.
Apply cost information using various allocation and accumulation methods.
Analyze relevant information for management decision-making.

rows.title: Concepts of Criminal Law
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Interpret the concept of corpus delicti and how it informs the prosecution of general crimes, crimes against people, and property crimes.
Discuss the principles of constitutional law (Bill of Rights), and how the three branches of government administer those guidelines.
Utilize the California Penal Code to interpret basic criminal law terminology.
Explore arrest, search, and seizure principles, and the effect statutory and case law has on law enforcement practices.

rows.title: Introduction to Administration of Justice
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Explain traditional and contemporary theories of crime and criminal behavior.
Distinguish the levels of criminal offense and the possible pathways of a criminal suspect through the criminal justice system.
Explain the structure and functions of the California and federal court systems and the factors that affect sentencing in those systems.
Identify and critique modern problems in the criminal justice system.

rows.title: Progressive Policing in the 21st Century
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze the history of community policing in the contexts of race and class.
Explain the intersection of police, leadership, and community organizational models in the traditional and progressive policing eras.
Examine how both crime and fear inform progressive policing.
Describe the evolution of progressive policing techniques, their implementation, and efficacy.

rows.title: Criminal Justice Report Writing
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Gather complete and relevant information from victims, suspects, and witnesses for useful field notes.
Write organized reports that are clear and mechanically correct.
Use the professional codes and conventions of criminal justice communications.

rows.title: Police Work Experience
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Execute the practical and typical duties of a Police Officer as assigned while working under direct or indirect supervision.
Apply the theory, techniques, and knowledge gained in the law enforcement curriculum in a positive manner.
Utilize radio communications and police equipment in a proper and safe manner.
Exhibit professional behavior as it relates to the law enforcement code of ethics.

rows.title: P.C. 832 Arrest and Control Certification
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply the perspective of a law enforcement officer to distinguish professionalism, ethics, and the components of a community policing program.

Analyze the differences between the powers of arrest of a private person and a peace officer, evaluating the laws of evidence and their relationship to U.S. Constitutional Amendments and the criminal justice system.
Produce a written police report containing the proper information from a crime scene.
Apply proper handcuffing, search, arrest, and control techniques, following POST standards and keeping within the guidelines of force relative to reasonable and lethal force.

rows.title: From Funk to Hip Hop
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze the social condition of Black people expressed in various syntheses, adaptations, and genres of Black popular music.
Explain the social and cultural links and messages of solidarity and resistance for racial justice between Black music before and since the birth of the hip-hop era of the 1980s.
Analyze how popular Black musicians impacted liberation movements by calling out systemic racism and racial injustice.
Evaluate the importance of culturally expressive styles and the socio-political implications of Black popular music on U.S. race relations.
Assess the rich historical connections between musical migrations, cultural interchanges, and the intersectionality of race and gender that gave rise to hip hop.

rows.title: Biological Anthropology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify the biological and environmental factors responsible for modern human variation.
Define the scope, focus, and subdisciplines of biological anthropology.
Analyze simple problems in human genetics.
Compare the morphology, evolution, classification, and behavior of non-human primates.
Evaluate the fossil evidence for hominin evolution using the methods and theories of archaeology and paleoanthropology.

rows.title: Biological Anthropology Laboratory
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply the scientific method to basic research questions in biological anthropology.
Apply knowledge of human genetics to problem solving in Mendelian, non-Mendelian, and population genetics.
Perform and record scientific measurements of human variation.
Describe, measure, and analyze contemporary and fossil human and non-human primate skeletal material.
Observe and record characteristics of primate behavior.

rows.title: Introduction to Social and Cultural Anthropology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify and analyze cross-cultural variations in the diverse ways of life around the world
Compare the field of cultural anthropology to the other sub-fields of anthropology
Apply the methods of anthropological research and cultural description while applying ethics-based principles
Analyze the major theoretical perspectives and concepts of cultural anthropology

rows.title: Magic, Witchcraft, and Religion
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe the anthropology of religion and its primary concerns.
Analyze and evaluate the theories and contributions of major researchers in the anthropology of magic, witchcraft, and religion.
Utilize participant observation of a religious, spiritual, or supernatural ritual or event as an ethnographic method of anthropological research.
Interpret and describe differing religious and magical belief systems in a relativistic and holistic manner using ethnographic and/or historical examples.

rows.title: Architecture Design Studio III
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Create architectural solutions to a set of project requirements
Produce documents analyzing various aspects of the urban environment
Analyze the impact of programmatic requirements and site parameters in the design process
Communicate the design process visually, orally, in writing, and by models (physical and digital)

rows.title: Architectural Graphics I
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze systems used in architectural design drawings.
Create orthographic, paraline and perspective drawings that communicate simple architectural design intentions.
Use both analog and digital drawing tools and understand their affect and potential for graphic communication.
Interpret the correct use of architectural scale, drawing symbols, line weights, and line types that follow architectural graphic conventions.

rows.title: Fundamentals of the International Building Code
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Explain the history and purpose of model building codes including how they are developed, managed, kept up to date, and enforced.
Analyze how provisions of the IBC can apply to the design and planning of various building types.
Apply appropriate research methods to conduct building code research relevant to architectural projects.

rows.title: History of Architecture II
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Compare significant features, characteristics and representative buildings of various architectural movements since 1400 C.E. using accurate terminology and interpreted through visual environmental literacy.
Evaluate how cultural, climatic, ecological, technological, socioeconomic, and public health conditions have impacted the design of the built environment since 1400 C.E.
Analyze the ways architecture has served diverse human needs, values, and aspirations since 1400 C.E.

rows.title: African-American Art History
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Employ historical and visual literacy methods in order to analyze African and African American art and architecture.
Compare and distinguish styles, trends, periods and art movements in African and African-American art
Evaluate works of art with regard to their social, political, and cultural contexts.
Discuss works of art by pivotal African and African-American artists.
Analyze African American and Afro-centered thematic, content and formal stylistic elements created by Africans and African-Americans.

rows.title: Arts of Africa, Oceania, and Indigenous North America
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify and analyze the formal visual elements and techniques of individual works of art in different media.
Compare the stylistic aspects and trends in the art of Africa, Oceania, and Indigenous North America.
Evaluate and differentiate works of art in relation to the historical and cultural contexts in which they were created.
Analyze the historical roles and functions of art, architecture, and the artist.

rows.title: 19th-Century Painting
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze and differentiate 19th-century paintings with reference to formal elements and style.
Identify connections between 19th-century art and ideas.
Analyze the social functions of art in the 19th century.
Evaluate the historical significance of individual works of 19th-century art.

rows.title: Basic Drawing
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply beginning-level drawing techniques effectively using a range of materials.
Utilize drawing concepts to effectively and creatively solve problems at the beginning level.
Analyze drawings from diverse cultures with regard to formal qualities and social and historical aspects.
Evaluate one’s own beginning-level drawings and the work of peers in terms of formal qualities and communicative aspects.

rows.title: Introduction to Illustration
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify principal areas in the field of illustration, considering foundational cultural, historical contexts and contemporary issues.
Solve illustrative problems effectively and creatively at a beginning level.
Apply beginning-level dry and wet material techniques in support of content.
Analyze illustration work using beginning-level design principles and illustration vocabulary to evaluate content and artistic expression.

rows.title: Beginning Watercolor Painting
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze the variety of watercolor pigments and painting processes.
Apply brushwork skills with paint effectively on paper.
Create textures using varying methods and additive mediums.
Solve basic painting errors using correcting techniques.
Apply vocabulary of watercolor when critiquing paintings.
Mix colors using basic color theory as a guide.

rows.title: Intermediate Intaglio and Relief Printmaking
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze contemporary and historical prints of diverse cultures.
Use intermediate intaglio and relief plate making techniques to create print editions that exhibit a development of imagery and technique.
Use intermediate intaglio and relief printing techniques to create print editions that exhibit a development of imagery and technique.
Analyze, evaluate, and revise work based on proofing and critiques.
Practice safe working methods when using equipment, tools, and supplies.

rows.title: Intermediate Sculpture
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Practice safe working methods when using sculpture tools and materials.
Evaluate technical aspects, composition, craft, material choice, and content when discussing sculptural forms.
Produce artwork that demonstrates intermediate understanding of additive and subtractive sculptural processes using applicable tools and materials.

rows.title: Introduction to Asian American Studies
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze and investigate critical ethnic studies concepts including race, ethnicity, equity, anticolonization, eurocentrism, Orientalism, and settler colonialism, and other racially constructed power structures as conceptual contexts for studying Asian American histories and current issues.
Identify and analyze relevant U.S. governmental actions, law, and policies, and their impacts on Asian Americans past and present.

Analyze with relevant theory produced by and about Asian American communities the intersectionality of Asian American lived experiences along various vectors of identity, including race and ethnicity, gender and sexuality, socioeconomic class and labor, national origin, mixed heritages, religion/spirituality, generation, age, and ability.

Review critically how Asian American social justice and political activism, resistance to Eurocentric racialization, and solidarity, from early immigration to the present, are relevant to current and structural issues.

Engage actively with anti-racist, anti-colonial issues, theories, practices, and movements in Asian American communities, applying knowledge and service ethics towards diversity and equity in and out of the classroom.
Analyze the term "Asian American" as a category constructed in response to legal and social exclusion.

rows.title: Asian Americans and American Ideals and Institutions
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Review critically how Asian Pacific Americans gained growing citizenship rights and obligations, including applying concepts and theories of race and equity.
Analyze how Asian Pacific Americans have exercised their rights and responsibilities as citizens, at local, state, and national levels, including histories of oppression and agency.

Compare how different nationalities of Asian Pacific Americans have historically been treated by the political process and institutions under the U.S. Constitution and California Constitution, including Ethnic Studies and Critical Race frameworks developed to interpret these experiences.
Evaluate how Asians in America have been affected by the political philosophies of the framers of the Constitution throughout United States history.

Analyze how Asian Pacific Americans have leveraged the relationships of local and California state government with the federal government, enacting struggle and solidarity to challenge structural issues.

rows.title: Chinese American Community
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze the ways in which race and racism, ethno-centrism, white supremacy, struggle and resistance have influenced the experience of the Chinese American community over time.

Describe the Chinese contributions to the development of the multi-ethnic society in the United States and evaluate how these contributions have been a source of agency for the Chinese American community.
Evaluate the impacts of public policy on Chinese American communities, using Ethnic Studies theory and intersectional knowledge of race, class, and gender.
Apply theory and knowledge produced by Asian Americans to understand critical events, histories, lived experiences and social struggles in Chinese American communities.

rows.title: Individual Study in Asian American Studies
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Design measurable objectives to evaluate project progress.
Analyze aspects of the Asian American experience based on independent research.
Assess results of projects and make recommendations for further actions.

rows.title: Manga and Anime
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Classify the major historical events, individuals, and organizations in the development of manga and anime.
Describe major artistic and literary characteristics in manga and anime.
Evaluate the role of the manga and anime as a form of artistic and literary expression that reflects social conditions.
Analyze the connections between manga and anime and Japanese society using different academic perspectives.

rows.title: Stars
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply basic terminology from solar and stellar astronomy.
Evaluate claims and information concerning the Sun and stars for plausibility utilizing the scientific method.
Assess the manifestation of physical laws in the realm of solar and stellar astronomy including their integration into cosmology.
Compare the evolution, structure, and properties of the Sun to the different categories of stars, including their roles in the galaxy and in planetary systems.
Question how knowledge gained from stellar astronomy has affected humanity's concepts of the natural world.

rows.title: Auto Body Dent and Damage Repair
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe and employ shop safety practices related to automotive metal repair and refinishing.
Evaluate vehicle damage and explain costs of repair.
Apply the basic skills and tool use needed for entry-level employment in repairing a car or light truck with minor damage.
Explain auto body shop business operations and considerations.

rows.title: Body/Frame Straightening & Repair
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe and employ shop safety practices related to auto body and light truck frame repair.
Distinguish basic vehicle structure types and parts and know their nomenclature.
Compare types of measuring and straightening equipment and their uses in unibody and full-framed vehicle repair.
Apply straightening, aligning, and planning techniques for full-framed vehicle repair.

rows.title: Auto Body Maintenance and Detailing
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe and employ auto body shop safety practices with special emphasis on auto body maintenance, detailing, and glass cleanup and replacement at an introductory level.
Evaluate vehicle conditions and estimate restoration costs.
Apply skills used for basic auto body maintenance and detailing.

rows.title: Automatic & Manual Transmission
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Diagnose electronic control systems using appropriate test equipment and service data.
Diagnose and repair automatic transmission shift malfunction concerns.
Assess automatic transmission parts, operation, and nomenclature.
Assess manual transmission parts, operation, and nomenclature.
Evaluate and repair power manual transmission clutch systems.

rows.title: Automotive Heating and Air-Conditioning
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Diagnose and repair automotive air conditioning systems.
Assess automotive heating, ventilation, and air conditioning system parts, operation, and nomenclature.
Examine and analyze refrigerant types and follow proper handling procedures in accordance with environmental laws.

rows.title: Introduction to Diesel Technology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply appropriate safety procedures while handling diesel repair equipment
Identify the major components of a modern diesel engine and explain their functions.
Select and employ appropriate tools and equipment to perform diesel diagnosis and basic repairs

Evaluate overall vehicle condition and perform maintenance and light repair of diesel engines and related emissions systems in accordance with the National Automotive Technicians Education Foundation (NATEF) certification standards.

rows.title: Introduction to Writing for Electronic Media
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Illustrate various reporting and writing techniques based on the unique nature of each electronic medium by writing appropriately formatted scripts.
Analyze the various elements, styles, and formats of news stories and public service announcements in different electronic media.
Apply the fundamental principles of persuasive, documentary, and entertainment screenwriting.
Describe the technical and aesthetic issues related to writing for the electronic media.

rows.title: Pro Tools Editing Essentials
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Use Pro Tools software to perform industry-standard, editing workflow for music and sound design projects.
Apply theories of digital audio sampling, quantizing, and data compression output formats to digital audio projects.
Assess audio editing project operations and workflow while using industry-standard vocabulary terms.

rows.title: Surround and Immersive Sound Mixing
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Explain and evaluate the differences in surround sound and immersive audio mixing techniques.
Use digital mixing control surfaces with Avid Pro Tools software to mix projects in multiple speaker sound distribution.
Employ frequency-based, dynamic, and time-based processor software plugins in multichannel format to a final 5.1 mix and master.

rows.title: Video for the Web
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Produce and distribute video for the web.
Create video content that tells a story.
Use current technology to promote video content to target audience.
Analyze the differences between television and web-based video content.

rows.title: Video Editing Premiere Pro - Intermediate
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Initiate and complete video editing projects and asset preparation at an aesthetic and technical intermediate level using Adobe Premiere Pro
Analyze and apply digital video effects, titles, and object movement relative to and appropriate for a project at an intermediate level
Analyze and apply common video editing finishing techniques to enhance a video program at an intermediate level using Adobe Premiere Pro
Analyze and apply video compression to video projects and assets appropriate to the delivery type at an intermediate level using Adobe Premiere Pro and Media Encoder

rows.title: Intermediate Field Video Production
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Operate professional video, audio, lighting, and other common video production equipment proficiently and safely.
Collaborate on and execute common field video pre-production organizational and assessment tasks.
Evaluate and apply video recording formats and common techniques to video production and editing.
Produce video content from concept through production to completion as a member of a collaborative team, suitable for broadcast, commercial, and/or institutional outlets.

rows.title: Revit Architecture I
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Evaluate the benefits and challenges of using Building Information Modeling (BIM) for building design and construction.

Apply Revit Architecture software tools to develop a three-dimensional digital model and architectural drawing set of a building using the standards and conventions of architectural graphic representation.
Explain the use of the various tools in Revit Architecture software to effectively collaborate with others in Building Information Modeling (BIM).

rows.title: Introduction to Human Anatomy and Physiology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Recognize and develop a vocabulary of appropriate terminology effectively communicating information related to anatomy and physiology.
Explain concepts associated with human physiological functions from cells to body systems, including homeostasis and the use of feedback loops to control physiological systems.
Formulate concepts to make connections between anatomy and physiology and real-world situations.
Use laboratory procedures to collect and analyze data to examine and evaluate anatomical structures and physiological functions.

rows.title: Introduction to Human Physiology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Use the basic terminology and concepts of human physiology to describe the mechanisms of normal physiological processes.
Construct the relationship between different physiological mechanisms necessary to create a working homeostatic system.
Apply the concepts and principles of hypothesis testing, using physiological laboratory skills to compare normal human physiological function and variability.
Construct and communicate an argument for physiological mechanisms using collected laboratory data.

rows.title: Plant Biology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify the molecular, cellular, and anatomical components of plants.
Describe plant physiological mechanisms, including metabolism, water relations, transport, growth, and development.
Compare form and function for the major plant phyla and correlate this to the evolution of land plants.
Synthesize evidence supporting evolution as the mechanism for the diversity of life and distinguishing diverse forms of life, including prokaryotes, protists, fungi, and plants.
Investigate and describe the ecological role of plants and their relationship with other organisms, including bacteria, fungi and animals.

rows.title: Introduction to Nutrition
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Employ science-based evidence when critiquing nutrition-relevant theories.
Justify dietary recommendations in relation to digestive health and metabolic diseases.
Analyze the relationship between dietary choices, nutrient metabolism, and health.
Examine the impact of food safety and security on health policy.
Integrate sociological and psychological considerations into perspectives on nutrition science.

rows.title: Ecology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe basic scientific and ecological concepts on a variety of scales and levels of organization.
Evaluate research methods used by scientists, particularly ecologists, and the validity of published scientific research.
Analyze biotic and abiotic factors shaping ecosystems, community structure, population dynamics, and species' adaptations, particularly on the local level.
Apply models to explain the behavior of commonly occurring ecological phenomena.
Apply ecological theory and concepts in practical applications.

rows.title: Ecology of Golden Gate National Recreation Area
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify key drivers and processes that affect community structure and dynamics of GGNRA ecosystems
Understand and apply ecological concepts to management issues faced within the GGNRA.
Evaluate scientific information and apply it in the field to specific ecological observations.
Observe and identify the diversity of habitats within the GGNRA and their associated fauna and flora.

rows.title: Agroecology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Compare and contrast the effect of industrialized and sustainable agriculture on ecosystem services.
Evaluate sustainable farming methods employed by Bay Area farms.
Assess personal food choices ranked by their environmental impact.

rows.title: Introduction to Conservation Biology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Summarize the full range of biodiversity on Earth.
Evaluate the ecological and economic impacts of biodiversity conservation and loss.
Appraise practical approaches to prevent species' extinction, maintain genetic diversity, protect and restore biological communities and associated ecosystem function.
Summarize how conservation biologists apply various experimental methods to generate data and form conclusions.
Investigate human impacts on species, genetic variation, and ecosystems.

rows.title: Human Biology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Critique scientific information in the media for accuracy and reliability.
Apply scientific method to laboratory investigations including designing experiments and interpreting quantitative information using graphs.
Relate the structure and function of the building blocks of life from microscopic to macroscopic levels.
Integrate the effects of genetic and environmental influences on health and evolution.
Explain the flow of chemicals and energy through living and non-living systems.
Evaluate the impact of humans on the environment.

rows.title: Molecular and Cell Biotechnology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply basic techniques such as micropipetting and spectroscopy to analyze and manipulate proteins, and mammalian and bacterial cells.
Perform advanced techniques of cell and protein analysis including enzyme assays and stable transfections.
Describe theoretical concepts of proteins, cell biology, and ethics that are relevant to the biotechnology industry.
Create an accurate record of lab work and results of cell biology and protein chemistry experiments.
Apply critical thinking to analyze cell biology and protein chemistry experiments.

rows.title: Career Exploration in Bioscience
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze and appraise various bioscience career fields, the required skills and educational paths.
Develop career skills needed for internship and job searches.
Research, identify, and target bioscience industry organizations and professionals for networking.
Synthesize and summarize a bioscience-related topic in a poster and present it to industry professionals.

rows.title: Advanced Stem Cell Internship Support
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Design and interpret the results of a novel and specific scientific research project.
Select and employ industry standard computer-based tools and resources to research scientific topics.
Create and deliver a scientific poster presentation to present original research.
Communicate scientific research and goals to multiple audiences with different levels of scientific proficiency.

rows.title: Analytical PCR Technology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe the underlying theory of advanced PCR methods.
Design and perform advanced PCR methods, including real time PCR.
Interpret and analyze PCR results using evidence and reasoning to support a conclusion.
Apply knowledge of real-time PCR to answer biological questions.

rows.title: Introduction to Technical Drawing
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Create freehand sketches of multiview drawings, including standard and non-standard views, auxiliary views, and section views, complete with technical lettering and accurate line work.
Create freehand sketches of isometric and oblique pictorials, complete with technical lettering and accurate linework.
Synthesize dimensions into technical drawings such that they fully define the part and are in alignment with industry standards.

Calculate the appropriate scale for a drawing of a specific part on a specific paper size, and accurately measure scaled lengths of a part on a drawing, using the appropriate architectural or engineering scales.

rows.title: Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing (MEP) Building Information Modeling (BIM) in Revit
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Distinguish the various equipment and ANSI symbols for pipe, fittings and joint type and interpret pipe specifications with regard to size and class.
Relate the functions of various equipment in an HVAC and piping system.
Create plans and elevation of various industrial process pipe installations using Revit software.
Formulate a procedure to plot scale drawings of floor plans and elevations of both pipe & HVAC systems.
Design HVAC systems for a building of specified square footage and calculate the size of components and ducts.
Create isometric piping diagrams and piping spool drawings, complete with bill of materials.

rows.title: Introduction to Hospitality
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Summarize hospitality as a field and philosophy, its evolution, history, cross-cultural dimensions, and interface with tourism.
Compare the possible career paths within the hospitality field by classifying the organization, structure, and functional areas of each sector.
Apply hospitality industry standards of ethics and professional conduct as they relate to customer service.
Identify personal passions, strengths, and abilities that align with career goals in the hospitality industry.

rows.title: Meetings, Conventions & Special Events
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Utilize common terminology in the design and management of meetings, conventions, and special events
Articulate the event-planning processes and elements
Create a theme and a space plan for an event
Describe the importance of sustainability in the meetings, conventions, and special events industries

rows.title: Meat Analysis
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify the various cuts and grades of beef, pork, veal, and lamb.
Explain the classifications of fowl, including chicken, turkey, squab, and duck.

rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Compare the major International Relations theories, emphasizing realism, idealism, gender, and constructivism.
Explain the organization of the international political system, including being able to identify international institutions.
Evaluate the role of national, international, and subnational actors, including nonstate actors, corporations, and non-governmental organizations in the broader context of lnternational Relations.
Apply International Relations theory to evaluate key contemporary subjects, including security, terrorism, human rights, and global environmental degradation.

rows.title: Psychology of Shyness
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze the behavioral, cognitive, and emotional dimensions of shyness within socio-cultural contexts.
Summarize the research and major theoretical perspectives on shyness and social anxiety.
Apply effective psychological strategies to address social anxiety challenges and to increase acceptance of shyness as a form of temperamental diversity.

rows.title: Research Methods
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Explain key psychological research concepts.
Apply research methodologies to specific research questions.
Critique research approaches through various lenses.
Summarize guidelines for the ethical treatment of diverse human and animal participants in research.

rows.title: Psychology of Gender
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Evaluate current research and theories on the psychology of gender.
Articulate how gender stereotypes impact self-perception, interpersonal dynamics and mental health.
Identify psychological outcomes associated with gender identities, including interpersonal relationships and the social world.
Describe and evaluate gender-oppressive systems and the resulting psychological impact and methods of response.

rows.title: Child and Adolescent Psychology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify and critically evaluate the various research designs used by developmentalists.
Differentiate the stages of development from infancy through adolescence.
Analyze and explain the different domains in which development occurs.
Evaluate the applicability of the developmental research and theory to diverse groups.

rows.title: Introduction to Psychology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Demonstrate fundamental knowledge and comprehension of major concepts, theoretical perspectives, historical and cultural contexts, and empirical findings within the broad discipline of psychology.

Use a scientific approach (including critical and creative thinking) to understand individuals’ mind and behavior within psychological, biological, sociocultural, and ethnocultural contexts while recognizing that biases filter experiences.
Apply psychological theories, concepts, and values to individual, interpersonal, group, and societal issues to demonstrate awareness of self and others.

Draw logical and objective conclusions about the mind and behavior from evidence to show how psychology evaluates, modifies, and supports its claims and counters unsubstantiated statements, opinions or beliefs.

rows.title: Fire Service Work Experience
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply Firefighter One knowledge and skills to emergency and non-emergency situations.

Use tools and equipment physically according to the National Fire Protection Association Standard 1001 for Firefighter One and the California State Fire Marshal Office of State Fire Training Firefighter One standards.
Define the importance of teamwork at emergency incidents and non-emergency training.
Assess patients and use appropriate medical protocols in an emergency response situation.

rows.title: Incident Command System 300
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe the Incident Command System (ICS) organization structure appropriate to the complexity of the incident or event
Explain agency policies that influence management of incidents or events in single or unified command
Develop incident objectives, strategies, and tactics
Implement an incident or event planning process utilizing the appropriate ICS forms
Create an incident plan that demonstrates build-up and expansion, demobilization and closeout of an event or incident

rows.title: Public Safety: Emergency Medical Response
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Explain the roles, responsibilities, and medical legal considerations of the Emergency Medical Responder (EMR) in the Emergency Medical Services (EMS) systems.
Apply patient assessment and treatment skills to a variety of emergency medical and traumatic situations within the scope of practice of an Emergency Medical Responder (EMR).
Perform effective interventions for adult, child and infant patients experiencing breathing, obstructed airway, cardio-pulmonary emergencies.

rows.title: Building Construction for Fire Protection
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify the fire resistance of building materials and how it correlates to building classifications.
Compare the different loads and stresses that are placed on a building for possible structural failures.
Differentiate the five building construction types as related to firefighter safety.
Explain the effects of fire and fire behavior on major building systems.
Analyze hazards associated with non-fire caused building collapse and the considerations related to firefighter safety.

rows.title: Rescue Practices
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Articulate fire service technical rescue apparatus and equipment used in the field.
Identify and describe the basic Incident Command System (ICS) components as they relate to technical rescue operations.
Examine the four tactical phases of technical rescue incidents and the roles of rescue teams.
Identify different technical rescues, associated specialized hazards of each operation, and basic safety practices designed to protect rescuers and the public.

rows.title: Company Officer 2A: Human Relations Management
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply appropriate human resources policies and procedures that produce company efficiency and successful member performance.
Analyze elements and consequences of the California Firefighters Bill of Rights Act, including disciplinary action.
Apply safety regulations in emergency and non-emergency situations.
Justify key components and consequences of the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996.

rows.title: Company Officer 2E: Wildland Incident Operations
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Develop an incident action plan involving resource ordering, incident facility location, incident report generation, and apparatus dispatch to sectors of the incident according to the National Fire Protection Association Guideline 1500.
Organize an emergency medical treatment plan for fire personnel based on local emergency medical protocols using the Incident Command System medical plan form 206.
Communicate with supervisors, crew members and other support personnel concerning updated progress reports on changes in conditions, fire behavior, and significant events related to the incident.
Execute wildland fire suppression operations and return resources to service as the incident is mitigated.

rows.title: Social Work Seminar
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe the major components of social work practice in the context of agency roles and functions.
Analyze how core principles from the NASW Code of Ethics inform decision-making in practice settings.
Examine current challenges in human services using critical thinking, problem-solving, and self-reflection.
Analyze personal practice in diverse communities through a lens of cultural humility and non-judgmental inquiry.

rows.title: Sex and Gender in the U.S.
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze the social construction of sex and gender
Explain variation among sex and gender beyond the binary
Describe the role of sex and gender in shaping social structure and inequalities in the U.S.
Evaluate the interaction between gender, social institutions, and culture

rows.title: Introduction to Cannabis Studies
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Distinguish sociological theories used in the scholarly analyses of cannabis use, regulation, and activism
Identify and evaluate different methodological techniques for studying the impact of cannabis on society and social relationships
Examine how cannabis laws, policies, and dominant social values establish and perpetuate social inequalities
Apply sociological concepts to current, real life situations regarding cannabis and society

rows.title: Continuation of Beginning Conversational Spanish
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply intelligible pronunciation and intonation at an intermediate-mid level when narrating in the present or past.
Apply accurate grammatical structures in Spanish at an intermediate-mid level to describe daily routines, give commands, or speak about past events.
Respond effectively to spoken Spanish with appropriate grammatical forms, accurate vocabulary, and clear pronunciation at a mid-intermediate level.
Explain the differences between aspects of Latin American and Spanish Peninsular culture and traditions by comparing architectural, culinary, transportation, fashion, and technological tendencies.

rows.title: Elementary Spanish
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Communicate in Spanish at a novice-high level with accurate grammatical structure, intelligible pronunciation, and intonation
Interpret the main ideas of a written text in Spanish at a novice-high level
Compose short written communications incorporating the principles of past and present tense syntax at a novice-high level
Articulate aspects of Latin American and Spanish Peninsular cultures

rows.title: Grammar Review and Composition
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Interact orally in Spanish applying complex structures, avoiding literal translation and English interference.
Produce a variety of prose using varied Spanish vocabulary, idiomatic expressions, and stylistic resources.
Apply a variety of colloquial and literary language registers in written and spoken Spanish.
Analyze and compare cultural, historical, and social aspects of the Spanish-speaking world.

rows.title: Spanish for Heritage Speakers 1
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Assess the grammar and syntax structures of the language by applying them to professional settings.
Communicate in writing with a broad range of vocabulary related to topics of personal, public, and community interest, applying enriched vocabulary and grammar proficiency.
Communicate and express with detail and some organization familiar and new concrete topics using high-frequency structures and personalized vocabulary that facilitate comprehension.
Describe and compare cultural aspects of Spanish-speaking countries as well as Spanish-speaking groups in the United States.

rows.title: Spanish for Heritage Speakers 2A
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze and synthesize Spanish grammar structures and syntax rules using linguistic knowledge, classifying words or concepts according to word order, grammatical use, and writing rules.
Communicate in writing using a range of formal and academic Spanish vocabulary, grammar, and sentence structures, avoiding interference with English.
Express thoughts fully and effectively in personal and public contexts using detailed evidence to support an argument or point of view.
Compare elements of history and culture of the Spanish-speaking countries in the Andean region.

rows.title: LGBT Voices in Hispanic Society
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze media in Spanish or literary passages in terms of content, plot, style, and cultural context.
Compare LGBT film, media, and literary characters in Hispanic culture.
Classify LGBT character representation and themes in media and literary passages within the larger context of Hispanic culture.
Integrate and apply, both orally and in writing, new vocabulary and introductory concepts of LGBT culture in Spanish.

rows.title: Continuation of Intermediate Spanish
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Communicate orally using an extensive range of vocabulary, sentence structures and proper pronunciation at an advanced-low level about social, cultural, and personal topics with a clear concept of human communication and interactions.
Evaluate ideas, arguments, and facts from written authentic sources using analytical techniques to assess the value of human thinking and creations.

Synthesize information by writing short summaries using complex grammar structures and accurate syntax and punctuation supporting ideas and arguments with critical thinking in an effective and meaningful way.
Analyze at an advanced-low level historical and cultural elements and issues from the Spanish-speaking world to interpret and describe societal differences and diverse viewpoints.

rows.title: Custodial Training
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify and employ responsible custodial management of tools and equipment.
Employ safe handling of hazardous and toxic waste and materials.
Identify and demonstrate appropriate maintenance practices for various floors and carpets.
Select and use safely various automatic cleaning tools.

rows.title: Design Fundamentals
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply visual design elements and principles to organize compositions and create meaning.
Analyze the quality and integrity of design work to evaluate the relationship between the audience, form, content and context.
Employ research, sketching, and ideation techniques.
Revise and improve a design solution using an iterative process, working individually and as a part of a group.
Employ design vocabulary to explain one's design process and outcomes orally, visually, and in written form.

rows.title: Design Drawing Techniques
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Explain the role and techniques of rapid visualization in design thinking and making.
Employ various design sketching techniques to explore design ideas.
Analyze and discuss the merits of using design drawing techniques for visual thinking.

rows.title: Information Design
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify common information design data types and structures.
Design and produce an information design that enhances the viewer's understanding of a complex topic involving multiple data sets.
Collect and analyze information thoroughly and responsibly while providing citations for reputable sources.
Employ critical thinking and communications skills in the development of information design solutions.
Employ and document an iterative design process.

rows.title: Typography I
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Employ typographic terminology, classification and typesetting conventions in design work.
Create layouts demonstrating how legibility, readability, and typographic hierarchy impact the design of effective communications.
Employ an iterative design process in individual and collaborative design activities.
Analyze various design solutions to determine the effect of typography on connotative and denotative messaging within a design solution.

rows.title: Illustrator I
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe the major components of the Adobe Illustrator user interface.
Construct basic Illustrator documents according to industry best practices in design and illustration standards.
Analyze and reproduce basic Illustrator files using appropriate tools and techniques.

rows.title: Photoshop I
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Construct basic files in Photoshop using industry-standard best practices.
Identify and describe the major components of the Photoshop user interface.
Analyze and reproduce basic Photoshop files using appropriate tools and techniques.

rows.title: Digital Illustration I
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Research source imagery to use as reference for creating illustrations.
Develop original concepts into images that clearly communicate intended messages.
Create original illustrations with both raster and vector-based tools.
Evaluate and critique their work and the work of others using relevant terms and concepts.

rows.title: Internship/Work Experience 1
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Determine employment opportunities requiring entry-level skills in the visual media design profession
Obtain intership by sucessfully applying, interviewing and showcasing portfolio
Apply visual media design skills as required in a professional work environment
Manage effective communication with supervisors and co-workers

rows.title: Home Health Aide
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Follow the agency protocol for infection control and utilize personal protective equipment in any patient care skill in a home based setting.
Identify the roles and responsibilities of a home health aide, including equipment to bring to patients home, safety and infection control in a home based setting.
Define applicable emergency procedures that could be used in a home setting.
Explain the difference between a home health aide and a CNA.
Perform patient care related to activities of daily living in a home based setting.

rows.title: Clinical and Skills Lab I
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify and utilize the proper techniques of medical/surgical asepsis with patients, supplies, and equipment.
Apply critical thinking and appropriate clinical judgment when providing nursing care and monitoring patients' conditions.
Employ professional conduct, appearance, and cultural competency.
Identify changes in a client’s condition or assessment findings and report appropriately.
Communicate with the healthcare team and document nursing care, including basic assessment and administration of medications.

rows.title: Clinical and Skills Lab II
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Assemble the appropriate equipment and provide an accurate description of the purpose of each adult medical surgical skill performed.
Apply the current standards during the satisfactory performance of each adult medical surgical skill utilizing at least ten (10) of the LVN Department's Standard Steps of Nursing Procedures
Explain the nursing responsibilities before, during, and after each adult medical surgical skill is performed and formulate a patient teaching plan that includes its description and purpose.
Perform hands-on assessment and application of appropriate nursing interventions for clients with medical surgical disorders.
Apply nursing care and interventions to clients with medical surgical disorders, utilizing critical thinking and appropriate clinical judgment.

rows.title: Manufacturing Processes
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe the operation and functions of basic machine shop tools.
Explain tolerances and their importance to part manufacture.
Assess and apply safe machine shop practices.
Perform metal cutting, threading, and surface hardening operations.
Describe metal coding and numbering systems.

rows.title: Introduction to Masculinity Studies
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Discuss how sex, gender expression, and gender identity function within larger economic and political landscapes.
Analyze how masculinities and masculine roles are constructed and how constructs vary according to systems of difference.
Evaluate the impact of dominant forms of masculinity on public health and societal well-being.
Analyze key cultural works aimed at resisting dominant forms of masculinity within and across different racial and ethnic groups.
Evaluate the effectiveness of organizations and social movements aimed at constructing new masculinities, particularly in terms of impact on interpersonal violence and gender inequality.
